"What is essential is invisible to the eye" – The Little Prince
summary: We developed Qhapaq Ñan, a navigation, geospatial intelligence, and mission assistance software ecosystem designed for human Mars exploration. We address the challenge through Khipu, a central geospatial processing and terrain analysis engine that coordinates three interfaces tailored to each mission environment: Hatun Wasi as the base command center that analyzes the Martian surface, evaluates risks, and plans strategic expeditions; Chaski as a tactical interface on rovers and mobile tablets that assists navigation, guides transit, and supports field decisions; and Ñawi as a spacesuit visor display that projects heading, terrain landmarks, and life-support status directly onto the helmet without obstructing the astronaut's view. This development is crucial because communications with Earth take up to 20 minutes, making remote assistance too slow during hazards. Qhapaq Ñan addresses this under three essential priorities: ensuring crew safety with guaranteed safe return, maximizing surface science discovery, and providing the mission with operational autonomy for immediate decision-making during Mars explorations.
details:
Qhapaq Ñan: Intelligent Navigation and Martian Exploration Ecosystem

Can an astronaut on Mars know with mathematical certainty whether they will have enough oxygen to return to base before taking their next step?

At 225 million kilometers from Earth, a communications delay of up to 20 minutes turns any unexpected event into a lethal threat. If a crew descends into a canyon or a rover becomes immobilized in loose regolith, mission control in Houston cannot intervene in time. Qhapaq Ñan is not a static map: It is an integrated ecosystem of autonomous navigation, physical risk simulation, and real-time decision support that guarantees survival, protects science, and grants total tactical independence to surface missions on Mars.

What Does It Do or How Does It Work?

The ecosystem operates under a strict hierarchy of operational priorities: Safety, Science, and Autonomy.

The analytical core of the system is the Khipu engine, which transforms orbital elevation maps into living four-dimensional navigation corridors (x, y, z, t). The workflow functions as follows:

  1. Terrain Synthesis and Space Physics: Khipu processes MOLA elevation models and Jezero Crater geology. Instead of treating the map as a static snapshot, it calculates the position of the sun minute by minute using Martian ephemeris (Mars24) and traces shadow progression across relief, projecting solar radiation availability for batteries and thermal stress.
  2. Telecommunications and Blind-Spot Evaluation: It models line-of-sight to base and knife-edge obstacle diffraction (ITU-R P.526 standard), preventing crews from becoming trapped in radio shadows behind crater rims, plateaus, or canyons.
  3. Human Biomechanics and Rover Terramechanics:
    • On foot expeditions (EVA), it computes metabolic expenditure scaled to Martian gravity (3.72 m/s²), oxygen consumption rates (20.1 kJ/L O₂), and muscular fatigue in pressurized gloves through the Rohmert isometric endurance model.
    • On vehicles, it applies Bekker-Wong sinkage and Janosi-Hanamoto shear equations to predict slippage, skidding, and energy consumption in Martian regolith.
  4. Rigorous Point of No Return (PNR) Calculation: The algorithm continuously evaluates whether a viable return path to base exists with a certified minimum safety margin of 20% in life support and battery reserves. If an astronaut approaches this threshold, the system immediately alerts and recalculates.
  5. Distribution Across Three Specialized Interfaces:
    • Hatun Wasi: Strategic habitat console to plan missions, evaluate multi-layer risks, and certify safe routes before egress.
    • Chaski: Tactical interface on rovers and rugged field tablets that monitors tilt, traction loss, and recalculates diversions en route.
    • Ñawi: Heads-up display (HUD) projected onto the astronaut's helmet visor, providing peripheral headings, safe corridor vectors, and vital life-support metrics without obstructing their geological field of view.


      To complement these interfaces in the field, the ecosystem integrates an intelligent voice copilot powered by the Google Gemini API. This complementary assistant interprets complex telemetry, answers queries in natural language, and provides verbal status briefings inside the helmet, allowing astronauts to maintain situational awareness completely hands-free without touching physical screens during extravehicular activity.

What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Guaranteed Safe Return: Exhaustive point of no return (PNR) computation eliminates the risk of explorers or rovers becoming stranded beyond the reach of their life support or battery reserves.
  • Elimination of Telecommunication Blind Spots: It routes paths that preserve radio line-of-sight or acceptable diffraction with the base, ensuring continuous transmission of medical and operational telemetry.
  • Energy and Thermal Preservation: It synchronizes movement with the solar trajectory, avoiding extreme cold shadow valleys and ensuring continuous photovoltaic recharge for mobile systems.
  • Maximization of Scientific Return: It weights high-value geological units (clay deltas, lacustrine sediments, and impact crater rims) as route attractors, optimizing sampling yield for every expedition hour.
  • Hands-Free Tactical Operation: Natural voice interaction powered by Gemini allows astronauts to query system state, receive terrain advisories, and confirm route changes entirely hands-free.
  • Ergonomics and Minimal Cognitive Load: It distributes information by role; field explorers receive subtle, intuitive visual cues in their helmets, while the habitat base manages overarching strategic complexity.

What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

Crewed Mars exploration ushers in an era where immediate assistance from Earth ceases to exist due to the 20-minute signal delay. If humanity intends to establish a permanent presence on the Red Planet, surface crews must possess tactical sovereignty over the terrain.

Qhapaq Ñan solves this critical challenge by delivering total field autonomy. By integrating geomechanics, life support, solar physics, telecommunications, and multimodal artificial intelligence into deployable local nodes (base, vehicle, and spacesuit), the project drastically reduces the risk of fatal accidents, guarantees adherence to survival margins, and lays the foundation for intelligent road and navigation infrastructure for future interplanetary civilization in Jezero and beyond.

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use to Develop Your Project?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3.12 (numerical computation, physical algorithms, and API), modern JavaScript (ES Modules, client-side logic, and interactive animation), HTML5, and advanced CSS3.
  • Artificial Intelligence and Intelligent Assistance: Google Gemini API (multimodal reasoning and natural language processing for hands-free voice assistance, verbal EVA status briefings, and telemetry synthesis).
  • Analytical Engine and Scientific Computing:
    • NumPy and SciPy: Matrix linear algebra, differential equation solving for terramechanics, and numerical meshing.
    • Rasterio, GDAL, and Pillow: Geospatial processing of altimetric rasters and topographic gradient extraction.
  • Physical Models and Specialized Algorithms:
    • Mars24 ephemeris engine and ray tracing: Dynamic solar modeling and insolation across relief.
    • ITU-R P.526 RF propagation: Spherical planetary horizon and obstacle diffraction models.
    • Minetti model adapted to Martian gravity and Rohmert isometric fatigue model: Bioenergetics and life support.
    • Bekker-Wong and Janosi-Hanamoto soil equations: Wheel traction and sinkage.
    • Arc-length subdivision search: Point of no return (PNR) calculation without monotonicity assumptions.
  • Backend Architecture and API: FastAPI, Uvicorn asynchronous server, and Pydantic for strict validation of telemetry and mission data.
  • Frontend Interfaces and Visualization: WebGL, hardware-accelerated Canvas 2D, responsive modular design, and adaptive typography optimized for habitat consoles, rugged rover displays, and helmet HUD visors.
  • Satellite Data and Official NASA Sources:
    • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) MEGDR ("MEGT44N000HB.IMG", 128 px/deg resolution, ~463 m/px) for topography and slope calculations.
    • USGS Astrogeology Science Center: Geologic Map of Jezero Crater and Nili Planum (Scientific Investigations Map 3464) for identifying stratigraphic units of scientific interest.
    • NASA Open APIs and InSight Mission Data: Atmospheric parameters and environmental calibration.
  • Infrastructure, DevOps, and Deployment: Git, GitHub Actions for continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) with automated unit tests for physical envelopes, and cloud production deployment via Azure App Service (Linux x86_64).

How Is Your Project Creative?

  • Translating Incan Qhapaq Ñan to Space Exploration: The Inca civilization connected over 30,000 km across the most extreme geographies on Earth not through brute force, but through intelligent topographical adaptation: establishing tambos (rest and supply stations placed at exact intervals determined by human physiology) and connecting them with chaskis (agile relay messengers). Qhapaq Ñan brings this Andean wisdom to Mars: Our Khipu engine functions as a multidimensional record of critical variables, and the software traces corridors connecting safe shelters and points of no return adapted to human biological limits.
  • From Static Maps to Living 4D Cartography: Terrestrial navigation systems assume a constant environment. On Mars, danger depends on the solar hour: Smooth, traversable terrain at 09:00 can turn into a freezing shadow trap with total loss of communications by 15:00. Qhapaq Ñan conceptualizes Martian terrain as an organism constantly shifting over time.
  • Tripartite Cognitive Ergonomics with AI Voice Companion: Rather than building a generic application that overwhelms an astronaut during intense physical exertion, the system distributes mental workload: The base analyzes large-scale strategy (Hatun Wasi), the vehicle or tablet assists tactical wheeled navigation (Chaski), and the helmet visor projects solely what is indispensable through intuitive peripheral vision (Ñawi). Furthermore, Gemini AI acts as an autonomous auditory copilot, answering questions like "Do we have margin to sample this outcrop?" with instant verbal calculations based on live telemetry.

What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  1. Communication Latency of up to 20 Minutes with Earth: All software, physical models, and analytical engines reside and run locally on Mars, ensuring immediate decision-making capability without relying on terrestrial servers.
  2. Pressurized Spacesuit Dexterity and Hands-Free Voice Operation: Astronauts on EVA wear rigid, pressurized gloves that severely restrict manual dexterity and make operating touchscreen tablets or physical buttons nearly impossible in the field. To overcome this physical barrier, we integrated voice interaction powered by the Google Gemini API, enabling crew members to request terrain briefings, monitor life-support margins, and confirm route recalculations entirely hands-free through their helmet comms system.
  3. Non-Linear Biological Expenditure in Spacesuits: Walking pressurized in a spacesuit weighing over 120 kg across steep slopes of loose regolith exponentially increases oxygen consumption compared to flat ground; the system couples slope energy cost into every leg of the journey.
  4. Risk of Rover Entrapment in Fine Regolith: Inspired by real historical lessons from Mars missions such as the Spirit and Opportunity rovers, we model soil mechanics to reject paths where sinkage or slip ratios exceed tractive safety margins.
  5. RF Shadowing Geometry: The steep cliffs of Jezero Crater block line-of-sight signals; the planner computes signal attenuation to avoid routing astronauts into canyons where they would be completely cut off.
  6. Visual Ergonomics and Sensory Fatigue in the Helmet: The Ñawi HUD design deliberately avoids floating windows, dense text blocks, or jarring alarms that could cause spatial disorientation or hide hazardous terrain rocks; it focuses on clean guide paths, subtle vectors, and unambiguous cues in peripheral vision.
